author: auhnalev
title: Last Z: Where Your Credit Card Is the Main Character
content:
I finally figured out how to win Last Z: Survival Shooter.

Step 1: Ignore the “Survival Shooter” part. Apparently that was just advertising.

Step 2: Take out your credit card.

Step 3: Keep taking out your credit card.

Step 4: Congratulations. You are now good at Last Z.

The matchmaking is probably my favorite joke. Spend enough money and you can become ridiculously stronger than normal players, then repeatedly farm them while everyone pretends this is “strategy.” Nothing demonstrates gaming skill quite like having a larger Visa limit than your opponent.

But the real masterpiece is what happens when money is involved. There are player reviews reporting paid packs not working, missing rewards and support tickets sitting unanswered. Even better, players who received refunds through Apple have reported getting their in-game credit/reputation reduced or their login restricted until the issue is resolved.

So apparently the most dangerous enemy in this zombie apocalypse isn’t a zombie. It’s requesting a refund.

Customer support deserves its own achievement:

“Sorry for the inconvenience. Please contact customer support.”

Achievement unlocked: You contacted customer support to be told to contact customer support.

And don’t worry if you downloaded this because the ads made it look like an action zombie shooter. You’ll still get some shooting between the important gameplay mechanics: upgrading buildings, staring at timers, collecting resources and being shown another opportunity to spend money.

The game actually has potential, which makes this worse. Instead of building a competitive game around skill and balanced matchmaking, they built an economy where spending can translate directly into power and weaker players can become resources for stronger ones.

Last Z isn’t pay-to-win.

It’s pay-to-have-the-privilege-of-being-destroyed-by-someone-who-paid-more.

1/5.

I’d give it zero stars, but apparently that’s the only thing in Last Z you can’t purchase.

author: Lady-Marine
title: Customer Support is not helpful
content:
I submitted a complaint to customer service about an interface issue that adversely affected my ability to reap the benefits of hard earned refugee fragments. My actual complaint was never answered, and no remedy was offered.

I contacted support after permanently spending a significant amount of refugee fragments on star upgrades for refugees that I intended to be among the refugees assigned to buildings so that I could benefit from their associated buffs.

To be completely clear, I never disputed that I manually initiated the upgrades. I explicitly acknowledged that in my correspondence with support.

That is not the issue.

The game has a large number of refugees. Only a limited number can be assigned to the relevant buildings and provide their associated buffs. Therefore, when spending upgrade resources, the important question is which specific refugees are currently assigned to buildings and which are unassigned. All refugees are listed with the upgrade arrow, further complicating the situation.

My actual question to support was very specific:

When I am on the star upgrade screen, what visual indicator, label, status, or other information tells me which specific refugees are currently assigned to a building and which are unassigned?

That question has never been answered.

Instead, support repeatedly tells me that the upgrades were manually initiated and that completed upgrades are irreversible.

I KNOW I CLICKED THE BUTTON.

I never claimed that I didn't click the upgrade button. I am saying that the upgrade interface did not provide the information I needed to know which specific refugees I was upgrading and whether they were actually assigned to buildings.

The resources were intended for refugees whose assignment would allow me to benefit from their buffs. Some of those resources were instead consumed on refugees who were unassigned.

I asked support to simply explain where on the upgrade screen I was supposed to see that assignment status. If the information was clearly displayed, tell me where it was displayed. If it was not, explain how players are expected to distinguish assigned refugees from unassigned refugees before permanently spending resources on an upgrade.

Again, I have never received an answer to that question.

What makes the situation even more frustrating is that support acknowledged the interface concern enough to say that my feedback had been forwarded to the relevant team for consideration in a future update.

So apparently the lack of clarity is important enough to pass along for the game team to consider improving.

But when I ask what happens to the customer who was actually affected by that lack of clarity, the answer is essentially: nothing.

The resources are gone because I clicked the button.

That is not a satisfying or reasonable resolution.

If the game interface does not clearly identify which specific refugees are assigned to buildings, then telling the affected player, “You manually clicked the upgrade, therefore it is your responsibility and there is nothing we can do,” completely ignores the reason the mistake occurred in the first place.

A future interface improvement does not remedy the loss that has already occurred.

I also made it clear that I was not demanding one specific solution. I offered reasonable alternatives, including restoration of the fragments, equivalent resources, or another account-side remedy that the company considered appropriate.

I was simply asking for the circumstances to be reviewed and for some reasonable remedy to be considered.

Instead, my individual case was declared final with no further review and no alternative remedy.

That is what I find most disappointing.

I can understand having policies about irreversible upgrades. What I cannot understand is acknowledging a potential interface problem, forwarding that problem to the development team for future consideration, and then refusing to provide any remedy whatsoever to the customer who experienced the consequences of that problem.

If the company believes the interface provided sufficient information, then answer my question and show me what information I was supposed to rely on.

If the interface did not provide a clear way to identify which specific refugees were assigned, then why is the entire consequence being placed on the player, with the only corrective action being to tell the development team about it for the future?

I am not asking for the rules to be ignored. I am asking for the situation to be evaluated fairly and for a reasonable remedy to be provided when the interface did not clearly communicate information necessary to make an informed, irreversible decision.

I did not need support to tell me that I clicked the button. I needed support to explain how I was supposed to know which specific refugees were assigned to buildings before I permanently spent my resources upgrading them.

They never answered that question.

And they never offered a remedy.

That is why I am extremely disappointed with this support experience.

author: Jdubbya80908
title: Pay to play
content:
Game is super fun, but you’ll need to drop some serious cash if you really want to be competitive/strong! 
You need to learn the strategy asap!! You will definitely waste most of your in-game resources on the wrong heroes, structures, technical training, and equipment upgrades etc; leading to stagnant play. 
Without paying $ for those modifications and upgrades to each equipment component and hero ranking, it’ll take years of dedicated play (hrs/day on average) to have a legitimately strong headquarters. On that note, game power doesn’t define your true strength. My power is at roughly 195k, but I’m regularly defeated by players with a lower power because they bought the equipment and hero promotion (stars) upgrades. Otherwise, that stuff cannot be acquired that quickly (non-paying players)!
Additionally, every Friday night, you better buy a shield (game currency) or kiss all your resources goodbye!! 
Once your headquarters reaches around level 25 (of 35), gameplay slows down too. Paying for construction workers and second lab helps with that, but your competitors are spending $100’s! Some spend that much monthly!! Also, because of what i mentioned and how easily you can lose all your resources, a lot of people quit, so that leads to a lot of inactive headquarters littering the edge of the maps. Usually they quit after being raided of all their wood, electricity and food, but another good reason is what I’ve mentioned. Forgetting that shield every Friday night, upgrading the wrong stuff (ex: technical training, lumberyards, farms, warehouses), and promoting the wrong heroes. 
The game is addictively fun, but you’ll have to pay to succeed. That financial advantage is why i gave it 3 stars. Otherwise, it’s definitely 4+ stars!

author: XD477
title: Toxic Players, Endless Spending Pressure
content:
I invested thousands of hours into this game and eventually realized the experience was built around two things: tolerating toxic behavior and encouraging excessive spending. Players who harass, bully, and create a hostile environment are often allowed to continue with little meaningful moderation, while ordinary players are left to deal with the consequences.

The monetization is even more concerning. The game constantly introduces new ways to spend, new power gaps, and new incentives that make it difficult to stay competitive without opening your wallet. It feels less like a strategy game and more like a system designed to identify spending habits and continuously pressure players into spending more.

I don’t mind supporting a game I enjoy, but there is a difference between fair monetization and predatory design. Over time, I watched good players leave, not because they disliked the game itself, but because they became tired of the toxicity, the lack of accountability, and the endless financial pressure.

I finally decided to walk away. The game had potential, but the culture and business model ultimately outweighed the fun. I cannot recommend it to anyone looking for a healthy, fair, or sustainable gaming experience.
